summary: The CDNI Metadata interface lets interconnected content delivery networks exchange the content distribution metadata needed for acquiring and delivering content. This proposed standard gives a downstream CDN enough information to serve content on behalf of an upstream CDN.

plainLanguage.summary: When one delivery company handles traffic for another, it needs instructions for each item: where to fetch it from, who is allowed to receive it, and how long to keep it. This document defines that instruction sheet and the way one company hands it to the other.

how does a downstream cdn get metadata
subtitle: The shared instruction sheet a downstream CDN fetches to learn how to acquire, protect and deliver another CDN's content.

tldr.problem: When one CDN serves content on behalf of another, the downstream CDN needs per-content policy: where to fetch it, who may receive it, and how to cache it.
tldr.mechanism: The upstream CDN publishes I-JSON metadata objects over HTTP. A HostIndex leads to per-host and per-path metadata, which carry GenericMetadata objects for sources, access control, authorization, caching and grouping.
tldr.outcome: A downstream CDN can serve content in line with the upstream CDN's policy, and must refuse content whose mandatory-to-enforce metadata it cannot enforce.

today: RFC 8006 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document itself notes that further metadata types and authentication methods are meant to be defined in separate documents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Content Delivery Network Interconnection enables a downstream Content Delivery Network to service content requests on behalf of an upstream CDN. The CDNI Metadata interface is discussed in the CDNI framework document along with four other interfaces that can be used to compose a CDNI solution: the CDNI Control interface, the CDNI Request Routing Redirection interface, the CDNI Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement interface, and the CDNI Logging interface.

The CDNI Metadata associated with a piece of content, or with a set of content, provides a downstream CDN with sufficient information for servicing content requests on behalf of an upstream CDN, in accordance with the policies defined by the upstream CDN.

The document defines a CDNI Metadata interface that enables a downstream CDN to obtain CDNI Metadata from an upstream CDN so that the downstream CDN can properly process and respond to redirection requests received over the CDNI Request Routing Redirection interface, and content requests received directly from User Agents. Specifically, it defines a data structure for mapping content requests and redirection requests to CDNI Metadata objects, an initial set of CDNI GenericMetadata objects, and an HTTP web service for the transfer of CDNI Metadata.

Only the metadata for a small set of initial capabilities is specified. This set provides the minimum amount of metadata for basic CDN interoperability while still meeting the requirements of the CDNI Metadata interface requirements document. The high-level functionality that can be configured is the acquisition source, which tells a downstream CDN where to fetch content from an upstream CDN; delivery access control, which restricts or permits access based on location, time window or delivery protocol; delivery authorization, which authorizes downstream CDN User Agent requests; and cache control, which controls the cache behaviour of the downstream CDN.

The metadata encoding is extensible so that further capabilities can be added later. The set of metadata specified covers only the initial capabilities above, and is intended to support CDNI for the delivery of content by a downstream CDN using HTTP/1.1, and for a downstream CDN to acquire content from an upstream CDN using either HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/1.1 over TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: One delivery company hands another the rules for serving its content: where to get it, who may have it, and how to cache it. This document defines those rules and the way they are passed over.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content:
The interface was designed to achieve five objectives: cacheability of CDNI Metadata objects; deterministic mapping from redirection requests and content requests to CDNI Metadata properties; support for DNS redirection as well as application-specific redirection, for example HTTP redirection; minimal duplication of CDNI Metadata; and leveraging of existing protocols.

Cacheability can decrease the latency of acquiring metadata while maintaining its freshness, and therefore decrease the latency of serving content requests and redirection requests, without sacrificing accuracy. The interface uses HTTP and its existing caching mechanisms to achieve that.

Deterministic mapping from content to metadata properties eliminates ambiguity and ensures that policies are applied consistently by all downstream CDNs. Support for both HTTP and DNS redirection ensures that the metadata meets the same design principles for both schemes. Minimal duplication improves storage efficiency in the CDNs. Leveraging existing protocols avoids reinventing common mechanisms, such as data structure encoding by using I-JSON and data transport by using HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: The design leans on ordinary web plumbing: cached HTTP responses, a fixed way of matching a request to a rule, and JSON for the data, so nothing new had to be invented.

sections.title: The Metadata Object Model
sections.content:
The object model describes a data structure for mapping redirection requests and content requests to metadata properties. Metadata properties describe how to acquire content from an upstream CDN, authorize access to it, and deliver it from a downstream CDN. The model relies on the assumption that these properties can be grouped by the hostname of the content and then by the resource path of the content. It associates a set of properties with a hostname to form a default set for content delivered on behalf of that hostname, and that default set can be overridden by properties that apply to specific paths within the URI.

To enable the metadata for a given hostname and URI path to be decomposed into reusable sets of properties, the interface splits the metadata into separate objects. Efficiency is improved by enabling a single metadata object, shared across hostnames and URI paths, to be retrieved and stored by a downstream CDN once even if it is referenced by the metadata for several hostnames or paths. Any metadata object A that contains another metadata object B can include a Link object specifying a URI that can be used to retrieve object B, instead of embedding B within A; whether to embed or to reference is generally a deployment choice for the upstream CDN implementation.

A HostIndex object contains an array of HostMatch objects that hold the hostnames, and optionally IP addresses, for which content requests might be delegated to the downstream CDN. It is the starting point for accessing the upstream CDN's metadata store, and it lets the downstream CDN deterministically discover which metadata objects it needs for a given piece of content.

The HostIndex links hostnames to HostMetadata objects via HostMatch objects. A HostMatch object defines a hostname or IP address to match against a requested host and contains a HostMetadata object. HostMetadata objects hold the default GenericMetadata objects required to serve content for that host, plus PathMetadata objects via PathMatch objects. PathMatch objects define patterns, contained inside PatternMatch objects, to match against the requested URI path. PatternMatch objects hold the pattern strings and flags describing the URI path a PathMatch applies to. PathMetadata objects hold the GenericMetadata objects that apply to content requests matching the defined URI path pattern, and their properties override properties previously defined in HostMetadata or in less-specific PathMatch paths. PathMetadata objects can contain additional PathMatch objects to define more specific URI paths recursively.

A GenericMetadata object contains the individual metadata objects that define the specific policies and attributes needed to deliver the associated content. It is an atomic unit that can be referenced by HostMetadata or PathMetadata objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are organised like a filing system: one list of hostnames at the top, then the rules for each host, then more specific rules for particular paths within that host, with the more specific rules winning.

sections.title: The Metadata Objects
sections.content:
The GenericMetadata object abstracts the basic information required for metadata override and metadata distribution from the specifics of any given property. It defines the properties contained within it as well as whether those properties are mandatory-to-enforce. If the downstream CDN does not understand or support a mandatory-to-enforce property, it MUST NOT serve the content. If the property is not mandatory-to-enforce, the GenericMetadata object can be safely ignored and the content request processed in accordance with the rest of the metadata.

A GenericMetadata object has a 'generic-metadata-type' property holding the CDNI Payload Type of the object it wraps, and a 'generic-metadata-value' property holding that object. It also has a 'mandatory-to-enforce' flag, whose default is to treat metadata as mandatory-to-enforce, a 'safe-to-redistribute' flag, whose default is to allow transparent redistribution, and an 'incomprehensible' flag, whose default is comprehensible. That last flag applies only to metadata objects whose safe-to-redistribute property is false, and signals to a downstream CDN that the metadata was not properly transformed by a transit CDN.

The initial set of GenericMetadata objects covers acquisition source, delivery access control by location, time window and protocol, delivery authorization, cache control, authentication and grouping. Source metadata provides the downstream CDN with information about content acquisition, that is, how to contact an upstream CDN Surrogate or an origin server to obtain the content to be served; the sources are not necessarily the actual origin servers operated by the content provider but might be a set of Surrogates in the upstream CDN.

The structural objects carry their own properties. A HostMetadata object holds an array of GenericMetadata objects and an array of PathMatch objects. A PathMetadata object holds an array of GenericMetadata objects and an array of PathMatch objects. Path patterns MUST be evaluated in the order they appear, and the first, and only the first, PathMatch object that matches the content request being processed MUST be used.

HostMetadata and PathMetadata objects form an inheritance tree where each node inherits or overrides the property values set by its parent. GenericMetadata objects of a given type override all GenericMetadata objects of the same type previously defined by any parent object in the tree, and are inherited when no object of the same type is defined by the child object.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of metadata carries a flag saying whether it must be obeyed. If the receiving company cannot obey a rule marked as mandatory, it must not serve the content at all.

sections.title: The Metadata Interface
sections.content:
The interface lets a downstream CDN retrieve metadata objects from an upstream CDN, either dynamically as required to process received requests, for example in response to a redirection request or a User Agent request, or in advance, for example pre-positioned acquisition initiated through the CDNI Control interface Triggers interface.

The interface is built on the principles of HTTP web services, so requests and responses are built around the transfer of representations of hyperlinked resources, and a resource is any object in the object model. Metadata servers are free to assign whatever structure they desire to the URIs for metadata objects, and metadata clients MUST NOT make any assumptions about the structure of those URIs or the mapping between objects and URIs. Any URIs in the examples are purely illustrative.

HTTP is the underlying protocol transport, and a server implementation MUST support the GET and HEAD methods. The HTTP response returns the status of the operation in the status code and the current representation of the resource, if appropriate, in the response body. Responses that contain a body SHOULD include an entity tag to enable validation of cached versions of returned resources.

In the general case a metadata server makes objects available via unique URIs, so the client first makes a GET request for the URI of the HostIndex. It processes the received HostIndex and finds the HostMetadata entry by matching the hostname in the request against the hostnames in the HostMatch objects. If the HostMetadata is linked rather than embedded, the client makes another GET request for the URI in the 'href' property of the Link object. It then inspects the HostMetadata for references to more-specific PathMetadata objects, by matching the URI path in the request against the path-pattern property items in the PathMatch objects listed there, and follows further links recursively until it has all the metadata it needs.

In cases where a downstream CDN cannot retrieve the entire set of metadata associated with a User Agent request, or has retrieved it but it is stale under the standard HTTP caching rules and cannot be revalidated, for example because the upstream CDN is unreachable or returns an HTTP 4xx or 5xx status, the downstream CDN MUST NOT serve the requested content. The URI for the HostIndex object of a given upstream CDN needs to be configured in the downstream CDN; all other objects are discoverable from it by following links.

Metadata objects MUST be encoded as I-JSON objects containing a dictionary of key and value pairs. Dictionary keys are case sensitive, and by convention any dictionary key defined by the document MUST be lowercase. The version of a metadata object is conveyed inside the CDNI Payload Type, either in the HTTP Content-Type header or in the JSON payload. All metadata objects use the media type 'application/cdni', and the CDNI Payload Type holds the object name prefixed with 'MI.'.
sections.plainLanguage: The downstream company fetches one index file, follows the links inside it, and keeps fetching until it has every rule it needs. If it cannot get them all, it must not serve the content.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious metadata server, proxy server, or attacker impersonating an authentic upstream CDN metadata interface without being detected could provide false metadata to a downstream CDN. That could deny service for one or more pieces of content, direct downstream CDNs to contact malicious origin servers instead of the real ones so that malware or slanderous alternate content is substituted, or remove delivery restrictions such as LocationACL, TimeWindowACL, ProtocolACL or Auth metadata, allowing access to content that would otherwise be denied and possibly violating licence restrictions and incurring unwarranted delivery costs. Unauthorized access to metadata could also enable a malicious client to issue metadata requests continuously in order to overload a metadata server, and could result in leakage of private information, since a malicious client could request metadata in order to gain access to origin servers and information about content restrictions. An implementation of the CDNI Metadata interface MUST use mutual authentication and message authentication codes to prevent unauthorized access to, and undetected modification of, metadata.

Unauthorized viewing of metadata could result in leakage of private information, because content provider origin and policy information is conveyed through the interface. A third party could intercept metadata transactions in order to gain access to origin servers and to information about content restrictions and usage patterns. Distribution of metadata by an upstream CDN to downstream CDNs could also introduce privacy concerns, since a downstream CDN accepting content requests might obtain additional information and usage patterns relating to the users of a content provider's services; content providers with such concerns can instruct their upstream CDN partners not to use CDNI. An implementation of the CDNI Metadata interface MUST use strong encryption to prevent unauthorized interception or monitoring of metadata.

An implementation of the interface MUST support TLS transport. TLS MUST be used by both the server side and the client side, including authentication of the remote end, unless alternate methods are used to ensure the security of the requests and responses, such as an IPsec tunnel between the two CDNs or a physically secured internal network between two CDNs owned by the same corporate entity. Once the two have mutually authenticated each other, TLS allows them to authorize each other, to transmit the requests and responses with confidentiality, and to protect the integrity of those messages during the exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrong metadata could send users to a fake origin server or remove a licence restriction, so the two companies must authenticate each other and encrypt the exchange.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document defines a set of CDNI Payload Types for the metadata objects, registered in the CDNI Payload Types registry, covering the structural objects such as HostIndex, HostMatch, HostMetadata, PathMatch, PatternMatch and PathMetadata, and the initial GenericMetadata objects such as SourceMetadata, Source, LocationACL, LocationRule, Footprint, TimeWindowACL, TimeWindowRule, TimeWindow, ProtocolACL, ProtocolRule, DeliveryAuthorization, Cache, Auth and Grouping.

It also creates a 'CDNI Metadata Footprint Types' registry, which lists the ways a location can be expressed, and a 'CDNI Metadata Protocol Types' registry, which lists the delivery protocols that can appear in a protocol rule. The initial protocol types are http/1.1 for Hypertext Transfer Protocol -- HTTP/1.1, and https/1.1 for HTTP/1.1 over TLS. Supporting CDNI for delivery using unencrypted HTTP/2, or for acquisition using unencrypted HTTP/2 or HTTP/2 over TLS, requires registering those protocol names in the 'CDNI Metadata Protocol Types' registry.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA holds the list of names for each kind of metadata object, plus lists for the location formats and the delivery protocols that can appear in the rules.

items.label: HostIndex
items.desc: The list of hostnames the downstream CDN may serve.

items.label: HostMetadata
items.desc: The default metadata for a host.

items.label: PathMatch
items.desc: A path pattern and its metadata.

items.label: PatternMatch
items.desc: The pattern string and its flags.

items.label: PathMetadata
items.desc: The metadata for a matching path.

items.label: SourceMetadata
items.desc: Where the content can be fetched from.

items.label: Footprint
items.desc: A location expressed as a footprint.

items.label: DeliveryAuthorization
items.desc: Rules for authorizing User Agent requests.

items.label: Cache
items.desc: Cache control for the downstream CDN.

viz.caption: THE STEPS A DOWNSTREAM CDN FOLLOWS (RFC 8006, SECTION 6.2)

items.title: Fetch the index
items.text: Make an HTTP GET for the URI of the HostIndex, which lists the hostnames the upstream CDN may delegate.

items.title: Find the host
items.text: Match the requested hostname against the HostMatch entries to find the HostMetadata for that host.

items.title: Narrow to the path
items.text: Match the requested URI path against the PathMatch patterns, following the first match, and follow links to more specific metadata.

items.title: Keep going
items.text: Repeat until every metadata object needed to process the request has been retrieved.

items.title: Refuse if incomplete
items.text: If the metadata cannot be retrieved in full, or is stale and cannot be revalidated, the content MUST NOT be served.
